# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–33 (Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Chapter 33 begins transition from events through Whitsun week (May) at Carbury Manor. Previous text covered evening of Tuesday following Fisker's departure (Saturday, 19th April) through Monday dinner at Caversham during Whitsun week (20th May arrival).
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton (harbor town); various American locations; Suffolk.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: All deceased as previously documented.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy, chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham. Strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter in "dripping white bonnet and shawl." Only Georgy and Jos present. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (godmother: Lady Jane) than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Devoted to children, especially Felix. Descended country to Dunholt village to escape eternal parties. Authored "Criminal Queens"—pandered to bad tastes through fabricated crime. Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. **Mr. Alf denies writing reviews himself; when judgment hostile to personal friend, he laments "accident." Lady Carbury disbelieves, correctly suspecting direct orders from Alf.** Proposed scheme to Henrietta: if she married Roger, Felix could inherit his name, title, property. Felix initially resisted but was persuaded; consented to remain another day at Manor House. Lady Carbury felt "almost unendurable nuisance" but deemed great effort necessary: ingratiate herself with Melmotte at Caversham dinner.

**Monday Dinner at Caversham**: At dinner, Lady Carbury sat with Melmotte; found him "heavy on her hands." He stated Felix "don't trouble me much, and I don't trouble him much" regarding directorship. Lady Carbury abandoned Melmotte, turned to Caversham parson (Protestantism enthusiast worked to enthusiasm by mention of Father Barham).

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful as star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Became Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Miles Grendall undertook to pay Vossner £450 at three months' end; Vossner produced £322 10s. in notes and gold.

**Sheepstone Meeting (Sunday afternoon)**: Met Ruby Ruggles beneath tree in grass meadow outside copse; spent half hour with her. Made promises and spoke of love though with contempt tone; found her appearance common. Before departing, promised to see her again Tuesday morning at kitchen garden bottom when grandfather at Harlestone market. **Resolved not to keep promise; planned to write asking her to come to London, sending money for journey.** Later, at Caversham Monday dinner, sat next to Marie Melmotte. Looked at her intently when she declared "nothing will ever turn me"; thought perhaps she would consent to run away with him. But considering trouble, expense, and risk (if Melmotte did not forgive and allowed her to starve), concluded "he could not afford to run away with her."

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable; admitted other reasons existed. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months but nothing further. Wore rose from Roger's room on bosom. When met Roger at door after garden confrontation with Lady Carbury, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Understands "tortuous mazes of manoeuvres" in mother's mind, disliking and almost despising them but refraining from rebukes. Not enthusiastic about marriage scheme for her.

**Roger's Renewed Declaration (Chapter 32 Evening)**: Walked with Henrietta, discussing church matters. Declared love anew, stating he is "constrained by the habits and nature of my life to confine myself to single interests" and cannot "escape from my love." Refrains from repeating "I love you" but says he "calculates chances" of winning her as man calculates chances of heaven. Believes she only possible mistress of his house; cannot live as other men do except as her husband. Requests she tell him truthfully if heart "absolutely given away elsewhere." Will not press sacrifice; thinks she might come to love him. Concludes: "If ever there should come a time in which you can say it truly, remember my truth to you and say it boldly...I at least shall never change." Abruptly departs. **Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken.**

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, close to Bungay. Had been to marry John Crumb (marriage postponed or abandoned). Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion; strong, healthy, tall; possessed own will. Though "utter fool," possessed principle; understood there was degradation she must avoid. Mistook infatuation for love when Felix Carbury came in her way "with his beautiful oval face." After Sunday meeting, resolved: "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife...I'll never be nothing unless I'm that."

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Arrived London from Paris within two years. Claims English birth though speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. Magnificent in expenditure, successful in business. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company with two million dollars of shares allocated to himself. Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and old Sussex property. In country during Whitsun week; no Board meeting possible. Invited Roger and Henrietta to Caversham dinner Monday. During visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour.

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well as foreigner; has begun forming own opinions. Absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Currently pursued by Sir Felix Carbury (claimed favourite in London). At Sheepstone meeting, told Felix "he might go to her father," deemed tantamount to accepting his offer. Resolved on constancy toward Felix; rejected other suitors. Felt complete happiness; expressed emotion saying "no one ever did it before." Promised to tell mother though acknowledged "Mamma does not care much about me." Said she had "never yet had anybody to tell anything to." Never formally pressed suit with father; deemed better to postpone until London. Blushes when Felix mentioned, fearing his faithlessness.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return to London from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him; Pickering could not be sold. Found letter from Georgiana on dressing-table (Chapter 33).

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Strong-minded protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London rather than be "buried" at Caversham. Had grudge against Lord Nidderdale; somewhat well inclined towards Sir Felix's prospects. **Chapter 33: Father promised return to London but now refuses. Georgiana felt "treachery"; would not have left town or contaminated herself with Melmottes but for that promise. Now told promise absolutely broken when impossible to get back to London without running away. Told father "you have simply and with premeditation broken your word to us." Father refused to argue, said he would speak to mother; ordered her away; she was "partly cowed." Meditated revenge; stood panting with anger, breathing indignation. Resolved: "I will do something. I'm not going to be cheated and swindled." Considered writing letter to father demanding removal to town or placement with Primeros. Most angered that family "should have condescended to be civil to the Melmottes down in the country."**

**Sophia Longestaffe**: Younger Miss Longestaffe. Presence of Mr. Whitstable at distance of not more than ten miles made difference to her. **Chapter 33: Georgiana's passionate outburst about staying down; Sophia somewhat reconciled to country sojourn as it inflicted fitting punishment on Georgiana. Was now almost reconciled because Mr. Whitstable's proximity made difference. Resented Georgiana's affront during afternoon silence.**

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings. Never persuaded by father or mother; has invincible will within own family.

**Lady Pomona**: Complained of headache (Chapter 33), excuse for not speaking. **Slept through afternoon's tension.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government; correspondence maintained with Mexican President.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

**Fisker's Departure**: Started Saturday morning, 19th April. Met by Nidderdale and Montague.

**Paul Montague**: Junior member of firm. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Met Fisker at Liverpool; travelled to London together next morning. Living at Beargarden; entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; champagne consumption increased. Could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at Carbury Hall. At Beargarden cardroom, offered to undertake Grendall's debt himself; disallowed.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase entirely belongs to Bundlesham estate. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Described as "certainly...a gentleman." Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words in confrontation. **During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance regarding established church authority. Later showed courtesy as host despite disapproval of Melmotte scheme.**

## Father John Barham
Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic; believes man should abandon reason to care of another or others. Faith sufficient unto itself; moral conduct testimony of faith. Meek at beginning, voluble with intimacy. At Sunday dinner, discussed Beccles morality with bishop, asserting "his people" more moral though poorer. Named Catholic families in county; proud of their fidelity; viewed them as "salt of the earth." In county only twelve months; knew nearly every Roman Catholic's name within borders. Engaged Roger in debate over church authority and bishop selection; suggested bishops lack fitness for spiritual guidance despite political success. After Roger's apparent exit from discussion, took departure to Beccles. Believed he had "sowed some seed" or "ploughed some ground."

## Property Relations
**Daniel Ruggles' Land**: Holds land on bishop's lease, Sheep's Acre Farm part of property which belonged to bishopric of Elmham, still set apart for sustentation. Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; thus one of Roger Carbury's tenants. Sheepstone Birches (wood/copse with narrow angle to road, gate leading to grass meadow) belonged to Roger.
